title: Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; Potential dividers; EMF and internal resistance
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Eduqas A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL07-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; EL07-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL07-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL07-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL06-uk1#N.3, EL07-1#N.3, EL08-1#N.3, EL06-uk1#N.8, EL07-1#N.5, EL08-1#N.5a, EL06-uk1#N.9, EL07-1#N.8, EL08-1#N.7a, EL07-1#N.12, EL08-1#N.10.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: NTC thermistor
items.clue: Sensor whose resistance falls as temperature rises.

items.label: LDR
items.clue: Sensor whose resistance falls as light gets brighter.

items.label: Potentiometer
items.clue: Resistance track with a sliding contact, giving any output from 0 to V_in.

items.label: Potential divider
items.clue: Two resistors in series across a supply, sharing the pd in proportion to resistance.

questions.stem: Three cells are connected in series in a single line: two of emf 1.5 V face one way, and one of emf 2.0 V faces the other way. What is the total emf of the line?
questions.explanation: Right. 1.5 + 1.5 − 2.0 = 1.0 V, in the direction the two 1.5 V cells push.

questions.stem: An LDR and a 300 Ω resistor are in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. In the room's light the LDR's resistance is 900 Ω. What does an ideal voltmeter across the 300 Ω resistor read?
questions.explanation: The pd divides in proportion to resistance: 6.0 × 300/(300 + 900) = 1.5 V.

questions.stem: A battery with an internal resistance of 0.50 Ω drives a current of 0.60 A through a lamp, and an ideal voltmeter across the battery's terminals reads 4.2 V. The lamp is then disconnected, so that only the voltmeter remains connected across the battery. What does the voltmeter now read?
questions.explanation: emf = terminal potential difference + Ir = 4.2 + 0.60 × 0.50 = 4.5 V. With no current, the voltmeter reads the emf.

questions.stem: A 12 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 12 Ω resistor. What is the current in the 12 Ω resistor?

A potentiometer has a uniform resistance track connected across a 9.0 V dc supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected between one end of the track and the sliding contact, which is one third of the way along the track from that end. What does the voltmeter read?
A battery of emf 9.0 V and internal resistance 0.50 Ω is connected to a 4.0 Ω resistor. What is the terminal potential difference of the battery?

A 15 V supply charges a 12 V battery. They are connected in a single loop, positive terminal to positive terminal, and the total resistance in the loop is 2.0 Ω. What is the current, and which way does it pass through the battery?

options.text: 13.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal
7.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's positive terminal and out at its negative terminal
1.5 A, in at the battery's negative terminal and out at its positive terminal

questions.explanation: Right. Net emf = 15 − 12 = 3.0 V, so I = 1.5 A. The larger emf wins and drives current backwards through the battery: that is charging.

questions.stem: An LDR and a 10 kΩ fixed resistor are in series across a 6.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the fixed resistor. The LDR's resistance is 50 kΩ in the dark and 1.0 kΩ in bright light. What does the voltmeter read in each case?

options.text: 5.0 V in the dark; 0.55 V in bright light
5.5 V in the dark; 1.0 V in bright light
1.0 V in the dark; 5.5 V in bright light

questions.explanation: Dark: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 50) = 1.0 V. Bright: 6.0 × 10/(10 + 1.0) = 5.5 V. The fixed resistor's share rises as the LDR's resistance falls.

questions.stem: Cells P and Q have the same emf. P has a smaller internal resistance than Q. Each cell is connected in turn to the same lamp. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The lamp is equally bright with each, as both cells have the same emf.
The terminal pd is larger with P, as less pd is lost inside P.
The terminal pd is larger with Q, as more of the emf is across its resistance.
The current is the same with each, as the lamp alone sets the current.

questions.explanation: Current = emf/(R + r) is larger with P, but lost volts Ir is still smaller, so terminal pd = emf − Ir is larger and the lamp brighter.

questions.stem: An NTC thermistor and a fixed resistor are in series across a supply of constant pd. An ideal voltmeter is connected across the thermistor. The thermistor is warmed. What happens to the voltmeter reading?

options.text: It increases, because warming releases more charge carriers in the thermistor.
It stays the same, because the series current is the same in both components.
It decreases: the thermistor's resistance falls, so its share of the pd falls.
It increases, because heating raises its resistance, as it does in a metal wire.

questions.explanation: An NTC thermistor's resistance falls as it warms. It becomes a smaller fraction of the total resistance, so the pd across it falls.

questions.stem: A battery of internal resistance r is connected to an external resistor whose resistance equals r. The external resistor is then replaced by one of resistance 2r. How does the potential difference across the terminals of the battery change?

options.text: It stays equal to its first value.
It rises to 2 times its first value.
It falls to 2/3 of its first value.
It increases to 4/3 of its first value.
